issues.description: Command name mismatch between Python and feature tests (underscore vs hyphen)
issues.detail: The Python methods are named `quickmarks_reload` and `bookmarks_reload`, but the end2end feature file invokes `:quickmarks-reload` and `:bookmarks-reload`. Existing sibling commands in this file use the singular form (`:quickmark-add`, `:bookmark-add`, `:bookmark-load`). The new commands break that naming convention and, more importantly, the underscore-to-hyphen translation needs to be verified against the command dispatcher. State the invariant: command names registered must match what tests invoke. As written, the analysis of name consistency is missing.

issues.description: reload() has no concurrency/atomicity invariant stated
issues.detail: `reload()` calls `self.marks.clear()` and then repopulates by reading the file line-by-line, emitting `changed` once at the end. The invariant — that observers see either the old state or the new state, never a half-populated dict — only holds if no observer reads `self.marks` between `clear()` and the end of the loop. If parsing raises mid-stream (a malformed line via `_parse_line`), the manager is left with a partially-loaded mark set and `changed` is never emitted, silently corrupting in-memory state. Build into a local dict first, then swap atomically, then emit. The literate comment should state this invariant.

issues.description: Test does not exercise the failure mode it should
issues.detail: `test_reload` overwrites the file and asserts the new contents replace the old. Good as far as it goes, but it does not test the more interesting invariants: (a) reload with an empty file clears marks, (b) reload with a malformed line preserves prior state or fails cleanly, (c) `changed` fires exactly once. Beware of bugs in the above code; I have only proved it correct, not tried it — and here we have neither proof nor a thorough try. A handful of additional cases would close the audit.

issues.description: Duplicated parse loop now lives only in reload(); __init__ is correct but the literate explanation is missing
issues.detail: The constructor previously inlined the parse loop; it now delegates to `reload()`, which is a nice deduplication. However, there is no comment explaining that `reload()` is also the initial-load path, nor that `_init_savemanager` must run after the first `reload()` so the manager is not asked to save a partially-loaded state. A one-line comment above `self.reload()` in `__init__` stating this ordering invariant would make the code readable without running it.

Both new Gherkin scenarios use a bare `Scenario:` header with no title. Existing scenarios in the same file are titled (e.g., `Scenario: Saving a quickmark (:quickmark-add)`). Readability matters here for the same reason it matters in code: a future reader scanning the feature file should see what each scenario tests without reading the body. Name them `Scenario: Reloading bookmarks (:bookmarks-reload)` and similarly for quickmarks.

review.summary: UNDER-AUDITED. The change is small, the algorithm is straightforward (clear-then-reparse, O(n) in file lines, O(n) space), and the data structure (OrderedDict) is appropriate. The refactor that lets `__init__` call `reload()` is a clean dedup. However, the analysis around `reload()` is missing: there is no stated invariant about atomicity (a parse failure mid-stream leaves `self.marks` partially populated and never emits `changed`), the command-name convention diverges from sibling commands (`:quickmark-add` vs `:quickmarks-reload`) and warrants explicit verification, and the test covers the happy path only. Fix the naming/test gaps, build the new map locally before swapping, and add a one-line literate comment in `__init__` explaining the ordering of `reload()` and `_init_savemanager`. The code is close to RIGOROUS; it needs the invariant stated and the failure mode tested.
